name: Aro Confederacy

summary.text: From Arochukwu, three kindreds in nineteen villages under the Eze Aro and his council, the Okpankpo, the Aro built a trading network across south-eastern Nigeria. It was backed by the prestige of their oracle, Ibini Ukpabi (the "Long Juju"), the high court of the east, whose losers were said to be eaten but were often sold, and by allied fighters from Abam, Ohafia and Edda. More than 150 Aro settlements and fairs at Bende and Uburu channelled trade, much of it in enslaved people, to Bonny and Calabar, and later palm oil. Britain broke the network in the Anglo-Aro war of 1901–1902; it set out to destroy the oracle, though its site survives.

snapshots.title: Arochukwu formed
snapshots.text: Arochukwu is born of the Aro-Ibibio wars: Igbo settlers of the Eze Agwu clan, the Edda priest Nnachi and the Akpa from across the Cross River drive out the Ibibio of Ibom and unite nineteen villages into one state. The oracle of Ibini Ukpabi becomes a court of appeal for a wide region.

snapshots.title: Nineteen villages and an oracle
snapshots.text: At home, Arochukwu is three kindreds in nineteen villages: Oke Nnachi, the line of the priest Nnachi, which holds the throne of the Eze Aro; Ibom Isii, of the old Ibibio kingdom; and Eze Agwu na Okwara Agwu, of the Igbo from Abiriba. The Eze Aro rules with the Okpankpo, the council of the town, which also sets the September harvest festival of Ikeji. Beside the town, through a gully and past a waterfall, lies the shrine of Ibini Ukpabi. Communities east of the Niger bring it their hardest cases, murder, witchcraft, poisoning and family quarrels, as to a high court. Those it found innocent went home; the guilty were said to be eaten by the oracle, and the red stream was shown as proof, but many were in truth led to the waterside and sold, and boats took them to Calabar.
snapshots.note: The oracle’s workings follow the Ibini Ukpabi article; the claim that its priests sold the losers rather than killing them is widely held but partly uncited there.

snapshots.title: The network spreads
snapshots.text: Aro families settle along the trade routes and run fairs at Bende and Uburu. Enslaved people pass to the coast at Bonny and Old Calabar. Aro fighters and allies from Ohafia, Edda, Abam, Abiriba and Afikpo give the network its teeth. Pilgrims from the Ijaw, Ibibio and Efik come to consult the oracle, which by then is sought more than Benin's ritual authority.

snapshots.title: The height of the Aro network
snapshots.text: Aro settlements such as Ndikelionwu, Ajalli and Arondizuogu become small states of their own. Aro traders reach north toward the Igala and Idoma country. After Britain bans the slave trade in 1807, palm oil grows alongside it. Commanders such as Izuogu Mgbokpo and Iheme lead Aro and Abam forces to conquer Ikpa Ora and found Arondizuogu; Okoro Idozuka widens it by war early in the 19th century. Aro soldiers found villages in Ozizza and help build Afikpo, Amasiri and Izombe. Baikie hears in the 1850s that Arochukwu is nearly three times the size of Aboh, its smiths famous for swords and spears, and that people say “God lives there.”

snapshots.title: The Anglo-Aro war
snapshots.text: From the 1890s the Royal Niger Company and the Niger Coast Protectorate collide with Aro trade. Sir Ralph Moor plans the attack from 1899. In November 1901 Aro forces under Okoro Toti sack Obegu, a British ally, and some 400 people die. On 28 November Lt-Col Montanaro marches with 87 officers, 1,550 soldiers and 2,100 carriers on four lines from Oguta, Akwete, Unwana and Itu; Arochukwu falls on 28 December after four days' fighting, and the British say they blew up the oracle; its site survives and is visited today. The last big battle is at Bende in spring 1902. Okoro Toti is hanged; Aro fighters keep up the war at Afikpo (1902–1903) and Ezza (1905).

today.text: The Eze Aro reigns at Arochukwu, Abia State. The Ibini Ukpabi shrine site is visited as a heritage place.
today.title: Eze Aro

reviewNotes: Aro settlement points (Ndikelionwu, Ajalli, Ndiokolo, Arondizuogu, Ozizza) come from GRID3 settlement names; who founded each, and when, is told in the event "The Aro go out".
The influence zone shows the allied Abam, Ohafia, Edda and Abiriba country; the network itself is shown by points and lines.

Whether the Ibini Ukpabi shrine was destroyed is disputed: the Ibini Ukpabi article says the stronghold was destroyed in the Anglo-Aro war, the Aro Confederacy article that it was not and still stands as a heritage site.
